chunks: "The slope of the inductor current is the voltage across the inductor divided by its inductance. That's di over dt equals v over L .
In the buck the voltage across the inductor is the switch node minus the output, so the slope depends on exactly three things: the voltage on the switch-node end, the output voltage, and L .
On the on state the switch node is at the input voltage, so the current rises at (V in-V out) over L : in my example 8. 7 volts over 4. 7 microhenries is 1.
85 amps per microsecond. In the off state the switch node is about zero and the inductor sees minus V out , so it falls at V out over L , 0. 7 amps per microsecond.
The things that don't matter for the slope are the load current, which just moves the triangle up or down, and the output capacitor, as long as the output voltage stays put.
The duty cycle doesn't change the slope either; it only decides how long you stay on each slope.

In reality it's a bit more complicated: the winding resistance, the FET drop and the diode drop all change the voltage slightly, the inductance has tolerance and temperature effects, and above saturation the inductance drops so the slope shoots up."
